questions.prompt: Which pair of RFCs defines the core DNS protocol — concepts and implementation?
questions.explanation: RFC 1034 (Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities) and RFC 1035 (Domain Names — Implementation and Specification), both from 1987, are the foundational DNS specs. RFC 4033-4035 define DNSSEC, 791/793 are IP/TCP, 2821/2822 are SMTP/mail format.

questions.prompt: On which port does classic (unencrypted) DNS listen, for both UDP and TCP?
questions.explanation: Plain DNS uses port 53 over both UDP and TCP (RFC 1035). For contrast: DNS over TLS (DoT) and DNS over QUIC (DoQ) use 853, and DNS over HTTPS (DoH) rides on 443.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum length of a single DNS label (one dot-separated component of a name)?
questions.explanation: A label is at most 63 octets; the top two bits of the length byte are reserved (they signal compression pointers), leaving 6 bits = 63. A full domain name is capped at 255 octets.

questions.prompt: RFC 8484 standardizes which DNS transport?
questions.explanation: RFC 8484 is DoH: DNS messages carried in HTTP/2+ over TLS on port 443, using GET (base64url ?dns=) or POST with content-type application/dns-message. DoT is RFC 7858, DoQ is RFC 9250, DNS over DTLS is RFC 8094.

questions.prompt: RCODE 3 in a DNS response header — what is its common name?
questions.explanation: RCODE 3 is Name Error, universally known as NXDOMAIN: the queried name does not exist in the zone. It is authoritative denial — distinct from NODATA (NOERROR with zero answers), where the name exists but has no records of the requested type.

questions.prompt: Without EDNS0, what is the maximum size of a DNS message over UDP?
questions.explanation: RFC 1035 caps UDP DNS messages at 512 bytes. EDNS0 (RFC 6891) lets clients advertise a larger buffer via the OPT pseudo-RR; the modern operational recommendation is 1232 bytes to avoid IP fragmentation (DNS Flag Day 2020).

questions.prompt: RFC 7816 describes a technique where a resolver sends only as much of the query name as each nameserver in the delegation chain needs to see. What is it called?
questions.explanation: QNAME minimization (RFC 7816, updated by RFC 9156): instead of sending the full name 'mail.corp.example.com' to the root and TLD servers, the resolver asks each level only for the next label (e.g. 'com.?' at the root, 'example.com.?' at .com), improving privacy.

questions.prompt: RFC 2308 defines negative caching. Which SOA field sets the TTL for cached negative (NXDOMAIN/NODATA) answers?
questions.answer_display: The SOA MINIMUM field (last field of the SOA RDATA)
questions.explanation: RFC 2308 redefined the SOA MINIMUM field (the last number in the SOA record) as the negative-caching TTL. The effective negative TTL is the lesser of MINIMUM and the SOA record's own TTL. Before 2308, MINIMUM was a default TTL for all records.

questions.prompt: RFC 9460 introduced two new record types for service discovery and endpoint parameters (ALPN, IP hints, ECH). Name either one.
questions.explanation: RFC 9460 defines SVCB (general Service Binding, type 64) and HTTPS (its HTTP-specific variant, type 65). They convey ALPN protocols, port, IPv4/IPv6 hints, and ECH config — and HTTPS records finally give a standards-based 'CNAME at the apex' escape hatch for web services.

questions.prompt: RFC 8020 is titled "NXDOMAIN: There Really Is Nothing Underneath". What resolver behavior does it mandate?
choices: A cached NXDOMAIN for a name means all names below it can be treated as NXDOMAIN too
Resolvers must retry NXDOMAIN answers over TCP before caching them
NXDOMAIN answers must never be cached longer than 60 seconds
Authoritative servers must include an SOA record in every NXDOMAIN response
questions.explanation: RFC 8020: NXDOMAIN is a statement about an entire subtree. If 'example.com' is NXDOMAIN, then 'anything.example.com' must not exist either, so resolvers can answer queries below a cached NXDOMAIN cut without asking upstream — reducing junk traffic to the roots (and helping during random-subdomain attacks).

questions.prompt: RFC 7873 added DNS Cookies to the protocol. What attack class are they primarily designed to blunt?
choices: Off-path spoofing and DoS/amplification using forged source addresses
Cache poisoning via name compression pointer abuse
Downgrade attacks against DNS over TLS
questions.explanation: DNS Cookies (RFC 7873) are a lightweight EDNS option giving weak but cheap transaction security: a server can require a valid server cookie before doing work, which off-path attackers forging source IPs can't supply. This blunts spoofed-source amplification/reflection and some off-path spoofing — without the cost of DNSSEC or TCP for everything.

questions.prompt: RFC 2181 clarified many DNS corner cases. According to it, all records within a single RRset must share the same value of what?
questions.explanation: RFC 2181 §5.2: records in one RRset (same name, class, type) must have identical TTLs; receivers treat differing TTLs as an error and should use the lowest. The RFC also nailed down CNAME exclusivity and what 'authoritative data' means.

questions.prompt: Multicast DNS (mDNS) lets devices on a LAN find each other without any server. Which domain and port does it use?
choices: .local names, sent to multicast on UDP port 5353
.local names, unicast to the router on port 53
questions.explanation: mDNS (RFC 6762) resolves names ending in .local by multicasting queries to 224.0.0.251 (or ff02::fb for IPv6) on UDP 5353 — every device answers for its own name. It's what makes 'printer.local' work. Corollary: never use .local as a regular DNS domain; mDNS-aware systems won't send those queries to your servers.

questions.prompt: You need a placeholder domain in code that is GUARANTEED never to resolve. Which reserved TLD is designed for exactly that?
questions.explanation: .invalid is reserved specifically to always fail resolution (RFC 2606/6761). Its siblings each have a different job: .test is for local testing infrastructure, .example (and example.com/net/org) are for documentation, and .localhost always points home. .fake isn't reserved — someone could register uses of it under a real TLD tomorrow.

questions.prompt: DHCP servers and Active Directory add and remove DNS records at runtime without editing zone files. What is the DNS mechanism (RFC 2136) called, and what opcode does it use?
questions.explanation: RFC 2136 defines opcode 5, UPDATE: a DNS message that adds or deletes records in a live zone, with prerequisites ('only if this name doesn't exist yet'). It powers DHCP-driven DDNS and Active Directory's self-registering clients, usually authenticated with TSIG or GSS-TSIG. 'nsupdate' is the classic CLI for it.

questions.prompt: TSIG (RFC 8945) is commonly required for zone transfers and dynamic updates. How does it secure a DNS message?
choices: An HMAC over the message using a pre-shared secret key, with a timestamp to stop replays — authentication, not encryption
It encrypts the whole message with the server's TLS certificate
It signs the message with the zone's DNSSEC private key
It wraps the transfer in an SSH tunnel
questions.explanation: TSIG appends a TSIG pseudo-record carrying an HMAC (e.g. hmac-sha256) computed over the message with a secret both sides share, plus a signed timestamp (default ±300s fudge) against replay. The content is authenticated but still travels in cleartext. It's unrelated to DNSSEC keys — DNSSEC signs zone DATA for the world; TSIG authenticates one TRANSACTION between two parties.

questions.prompt: Before RFC 8914, a SERVFAIL told you almost nothing. What did RFC 8914 add to fix that?
choices: Extended DNS Errors — machine-readable error codes in the EDNS OPT record explaining WHY (e.g. 'Signature Expired', 'Blocked', 'No Reachable Authority')
A new SERVDETAIL RCODE with an attached text message
Mandatory logging of failures to the zone's SOA contact address
A retry-after field telling clients when to query again
questions.explanation: Extended DNS Errors (EDE, EDNS option 15) ride along in the OPT record and give the failure a diagnosable cause: code 6 'DNSSEC Bogus', 7 'Signature Expired', 15 'Blocked' (policy filtering), 22 'No Reachable Authority', and ~30 more. Modern dig prints them as an 'EDE:' line — often turning a mystery SERVFAIL into a one-glance diagnosis.

questions.prompt: During a major DNS provider outage, many resolvers kept answering for affected zones with data whose TTL had already expired. What RFC 8767 behavior is that?
questions.answer_display: Serve-stale — serving cached data beyond its TTL when the authoritative servers can't be reached
questions.explanation: RFC 8767 lets a resolver keep using expired cache entries when it fails to refresh them — 'stale bread beats no bread'. Stale answers are served with a short TTL (recommendation: 30s) while the resolver keeps retrying upstream. It's why some networks barely noticed certain famous CDN/DNS outages. EDE code 3 ('Stale Answer') can mark such responses.

questions.prompt: Per RFC 9462 (Discovery of Designated Resolvers), what special query does a client send to discover its resolver's encrypted (DoT/DoH/DoQ) endpoints?
questions.explanation: DDR: the client asks its plain-DNS resolver for 'SVCB _dns.resolver.arpa'. The answer names the designated encrypted resolver with SVCB parameters — alpn (h2/h3 for DoH, doq/dot), port, dohpath URI template, and address hints — letting the client upgrade from port-53 cleartext to encrypted DNS automatically. It's how Windows, iOS and Chrome auto-discover DoH on supporting resolvers.

questions.prompt: Oblivious DoH (RFC 9230) inserts a proxy between client and resolver. What privacy property does that buy over plain DoH?
choices: No single party sees both who you are and what you asked — the proxy sees your IP but not the query; the target decrypts the query but never sees your IP
Queries become unlinkable to responses, defeating traffic analysis entirely
The proxy strips DNSSEC data so answers can't be fingerprinted
It hides which resolver you use from your ISP
questions.explanation: ODoH's trick is separation of knowledge: the client encrypts the query to the TARGET's public key and sends it via a PROXY. The proxy relays an opaque blob (knows your IP, not your question); the target decrypts and resolves (knows the question, sees only the proxy's IP). Plain DoH still shows the resolver operator both your identity and your full query stream — ODoH breaks that link, at the cost of an extra hop.
